summary.en: Use Euclid, Bézout coefficients, a prime sieve and modular inverses with explicit arithmetic bounds.
summary.bn: Euclid দিয়ে gcd বের করো, Bézout-এর সহগ দেখো, sieve দিয়ে প্রাইম খোঁজো, আর modular inverse হিসাব করো।

notes: The demonstrated programs use C17; the lesson states their input and arithmetic bounds.

sections.title: Shrink pairs and cross off multiples
Numeric size and bit size differ
No inverse is a valid result
Verify equations as well as answers
Use the invariant behind the formula

examples.title: Sieve every prime through a limit
examples.explanationHtml: Input twenty prints 2 3 5 7 11 13 17 19. Limits zero and one print an empty prime list. They do not turn zero or one into primes.

examples.title: Recover Bézout coefficients
examples.explanationHtml: Input 30 18 returns gcd six and coefficients minus one and two. The printed identity recomputes a*x+b*y so you can check the meaning of those coefficients.

examples.title: Find an inverse or explain its absence
examples.explanationHtml: Input 3 11 prints inverse four. Input 6 9 prints No inverse because their gcd is three. A negative Bézout coefficient is normalised before it is displayed as a residue.

examples.title: Read Euclid as divisions
examples.explanationHtml: The final program prints each division for 48 and 18. The remainder decreases until zero, explaining both the result and why the loop terminates.

practice.title: Find the inverse of 3 modulo 11, then decide whether 6 has an inverse modulo 9.
practice.statementHtml: Find the inverse of 3 modulo 11, then decide whether 6 has an inverse modulo 9.
hints: Begin with the state and the input conditions.
practice.answerHtml: 3*4=12 is congruent to 1 modulo 11, so the inverse is 4. gcd(6,9)=3, so no integer combination can equal 1 and no inverse exists.

quiz.prompt: Which identity supports Euclid when b is nonzero?
quiz.explanation: A number divides a and b exactly when it divides b and their remainder.

quiz.prompt: What does extended Euclid add to the gcd result?
quiz.explanation: Those coefficients satisfy the Bézout equation ax+by=gcd(a,b).

quiz.prompt: Where may the sieve begin marking multiples of prime p?
quiz.explanation: Smaller composite multiples already have a smaller prime factor.

quiz.prompt: Why are zero and one excluded from sieve output?
options: Neither has exactly two positive divisors
quiz.explanation: A prime has exactly two positive divisors; one has only one, and zero is not prime.

quiz.prompt: When does a have an inverse modulo m>1?
quiz.explanation: Bézout gives a*x+m*y=1 exactly in the coprime case.

quiz.prompt: What is the inverse of 3 modulo 11?
quiz.explanation: Three times four is twelve, whose remainder modulo eleven is one.

quiz.prompt: Which cost is appropriate for a standard sieve up to n?
options: O(n log log n) time and O(n) flags
O(log n) time and O(1) flags
quiz.explanation: Summing marking work over primes gives the log-log factor; flags cover the whole range.

quiz.prompt: What gcd does this remainder loop compute for 48 and 18?
quiz.explanation: The remainders are twelve, six and zero, leaving gcd six.

quiz.prompt: Which normalized residue represents the Bézout coefficient minus seven modulo eleven?
quiz.explanation: Adding eleven maps minus seven into the standard residue four.

quiz.prompt: After crossing off multiples of two and three up to ten, how many primes remain?
quiz.explanation: The surviving primes are two, three, five and seven.

An inverse modulo m exists exactly when gcd(a,m)=1.

examQuestions.question: State the invariant and justify the time and space costs of Number Theory Basics.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
For Euclid, a common divisor of a and b also divides a-q*b=a%b. Conversely, a divisor of b and a%b divides q*b+a%b=a. Thus replacing (a,b) by (b,a%b) preserves the full set of common divisors. At b=0, the largest common divisor is a.

Extended Euclid preserves an explicit integer combination. The recursive result is a correct equation in b and the remainder. Substitution gives the coefficients returned to the parent. The base equation a*1+0*0=a begins the induction.

For the sieve, every marked multiple p*k with k>=p is composite. A composite number at most n has a prime factor at most its square root; otherwise both factors would exceed the square root and their product would exceed it. That prime's pass marks the number, so no composite survives.

Finally, an inverse implies a*x+m*y=1 for some integer y, forcing gcd(a,m)=1. Bézout supplies that equation whenever the gcd is one. This proves both necessity and sufficiency, rather than treating inverse existence as a numerical coincidence.

Euclid uses O(log min(a,b)) remainder steps when both inputs are positive. Every few steps reduce the larger scale substantially; consecutive Fibonacci numbers produce the slowest classical sequence. If one input is zero, the result needs only the boundary case.

That is a count of arithmetic operations. With arbitrary-precision integers, a division is not constant-time, so a bit-cost analysis needs the operand lengths and the arithmetic implementation. The bounded long long examples use machine arithmetic.

The sieve performs about n/2+n/3+n/5+... markings over primes. The standard bound is O(n log log n) time and O(n) flags. Extended Euclid uses O(log min(a,b)) recursive depth and coefficient work per level. Inverse computation adds only coefficient normalisation after that call.
